source.title: Relating Misfit to Gain in Weak-to-Strong Generalization Beyond the Squared Loss

page_placements.theme: Theory refinements beyond 'must beat' (loss equivalence, bound tightness, limits under concept shift, boosting a weak generator)

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests weak-to-strong generalization with a different training recipe: a convex combination of logistic heads is trained to minimize reverse KL divergence. It reports the resulting test-loss and misfit outcomes, and gives theoretical results about when gain follows from misfit.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for its reverse-KL recipe, not a head-to-head comparison against naive fine-tuning. It cites Burns et al. and other work, but those cited results are not recorded as rows. Figure 2's extracted text does not reliably associate its plotted numerical loss and misfit labels with individual models, so rows use the paper's explicit textual comparisons rather than assigning those values.
record.test_reason: The study trains fixed-representation strong students (GPT-2 family; DINO ResNet-50 and ViT-B/8) on held-out weak labels (gpt2; AlexNet) and reports test loss and accuracy against the weak supervisor on 4 NLP and 2 vision datasets. This bears on V1, V3 and V6. It also proves misfit-gain theorems (V5). The recipe is non-standard (reverse KL over a convex combination of k heads) and is never compared against naive fine-tuning, so V2 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Two additions: on real data the misfit consistently exceeds the gain, which the authors attribute to realizability failing, and evaluating against the best strong model restores the bound. The authors also state their recipe guarantees nothing about accuracy and was not benchmarked against standard cross-entropy weak-to-strong training.
record.recipe_differences: Instead of standard cross-entropy fine-tuning of one head, the study trains a convex combination of k logistic regression heads to minimize reverse KL, with the strong model output in the first KL argument. It uses fixed representations and k=100 in the principal NLP and vision experiments; the weak supervisor is trained on true labels and then supplies held-out weak labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The discrepancy between misfit and gain generally decreases as k increases for all tested datasets except ImageNet; the authors note that the reduction slows at larger k. The reported size trend for GPT-2 students is increasing misfit alongside decreasing test loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Raising k (number of convex-combined heads) from 1 to 100 shrinks the misfit-minus-gain discrepancy on 5 of 6 datasets, with diminishing returns; there is no trend on ImageNet.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tightness of misfit-based gain bounds as a function of strong-class expressivity (k), not a PGR method gain.

record.problems: The experiments use fixed representations and linear logistic heads, and the weak-to-strong objective differs from standard fine-tuning. The authors note that the realizability assumption does not hold in their real-world experiments, which explains why the misfit can exceed the observed loss reduction. Empirical plotted values are not reliably associated with individual models in the extracted Figure 2 text; the reported error bars are based on 10 initializations.
record.rows_left_out: No cited results were included. The study's consolidated Figure 3d values and detailed synthetic-data scatterplot points were not separately rowed because they aggregate across datasets or tasks and do not identify individual model-condition outcomes in the text.

untested.parts: PGR itself: no strong-ceiling performance is reported, so PGR cannot be computed. The standard naive fine-tuning recipe is not run. Full fine-tuning is not tested (heads only, on fixed representations).
All of it. No auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling or loss-variant comparison against naive fine-tuning. The authors call benchmarking their recipe against the standard one future work.
Weak-supervisor size (fixed at gpt2 and AlexNet), chess, reward modelling, PGR scaling, and representation-based predictors.
All failure modes: uncheckable behaviour, distribution shift, and correlated weak/strong errors.
Vision tasks beyond CIFAR-10 and ImageNet linear probes; other modalities.

missing.what: Test accuracy of the weak model and of each strong student, per dataset. Weak: CosmosQA 0.618, Amazon 0.859, BoolQ 0.624, SciQ 0.597. Students: e.g. gpt2-xl 0.641/0.898/0.614/0.625.
missing.locator: Figure 2 panels a-d (x-axis labels and weak-model headers)

missing.what: Vision test accuracy. CIFAR-10: weak 0.803, ResNet-50 0.847, ViT-B/8 0.900. ImageNet: weak 0.559, ResNet-50 0.604, ViT-B/8 0.699.
Empirical finding that misfit consistently exceeds observed gain because realizability fails; the gap closes when losses are evaluated against the best strong model (Fig 3d).
Synthetic experiments where gain approximately equals misfit for c=2,10,50, getting noisier at c=100.

record.verdict_notes: Heads-only training on fixed representations. NLP accuracies are below Burns et al.'s full fine-tuning results. The ViT-B/8 ImageNet comparison with Burns et al.'s 64.2% is a cross-paper comparison, not a controlled V2 test. Figure 2 loss values could not be reliably assigned to individual models from the extracted text.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports test cross-entropy comparisons, not PGR values; it does not test the standard naive fine-tuning recipe or establish an accuracy improvement on every dataset.

No comparison tests whether auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, or loss variants raise PGR over naive fine-tuning. The k sweep concerns misfit–gain discrepancy, not PGR versus a naive baseline.

The study varies student size for GPT-2-family models and reports NLP and vision tasks, but does not vary weak-supervisor size, test chess or reward modelling, report PGR, or test predictors based on representations.
No tests of uncheckable behavior, distribution shift, or shared weak/strong errors.
The theoretical results concern loss gain under stated realizability, convexity or regularization, and optimization conditions; they do not give general conditions for PGR as defined in the claim.
Vision experiments are reported for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet; other non-language modalities are not tested.

rows.subject: Convex strong function class F
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 4.1 bounds target loss after projecting weak predictions onto a convex strong class using a Bregman divergence.

conditions.value: realizability, convexity, sequential consistency, and sufficiently accurate minimization

rows.measure: Target loss of the strong model versus the weak model, with a misfit subtraction and epsilon
rows.value: Strong target loss is at most weak target loss minus strong/weak Bregman misfit plus epsilon
rows.uncertainty: not applicable; theorem
rows.note: A sufficient theoretical result under the stated assumptions.

rows.subject: Convex strong function class F for classification
rows.operation_detail: Corollary 4.2 applies the Bregman result to cross-entropy and KL divergence.

conditions.value: realizability, convexity, and sufficiently accurate minimization

rows.measure: Cross-entropy of strong classifier versus weak classifier
rows.value: Strong cross-entropy is at most weak cross-entropy minus KL misfit plus epsilon
rows.uncertainty: not applicable; theorem
rows.note: The paper states that the exact minimizer satisfies the inequality without an epsilon term when it exists.

rows.subject: Convex combinations of k strong classifiers
rows.size_stated: k is arbitrary; error decreases as O(1/√k), with a class-count-dependent bound
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 4.3 bounds cross-entropy gain for a convex combination of k functions from a regularized strong class, trained against weak labels with reverse KL.

conditions.value: realizability and stated regularization condition on F

rows.measure: Cross-entropy gain over the weak classifier
rows.value: Gain is bounded below by KL misfit minus an O(1/√k) error term; appendix gives O(√(c/k)) for c classes
rows.uncertainty: not applicable; theorem
rows.locator: Section 4, Theorem 4.3; Appendix A.2, Theorem A.2
rows.note: This permits non-convex F through convex combinations, but the bound includes a finite-k error term.
